title: Roma Musical, Artistic, and Social History
grammar: Distributive frequency and allocation: -nként, -anként, -enként, -onként ('per / every / by')
goal: I can describe the rich musical, artistic, and social heritage of Hungary's Roma communities.
I can form and apply the distributive suffixes (-nként, -anként, -enként, -onként) to indicate rate, distribution, and cadence.
I can analyze traditional Roma craft professions, virtuoso Roma band traditions, and contemporary civic initiatives.

sections.title: A note on the words cigány and roma
body: Cigány is the older Hungarian word for the Roma, and it has been in the language for centuries. Roma (from the Romani word rom, 'man, husband') is the name that international Roma organisations chose for themselves at the first World Romani Congress in 1971; in Hungary it spread in public and official language from the 1990s.

Today laws and institutions mostly say roma: the 2011 Nationalities Act lists the roma among the thirteen nationalities, and the national Roma self-government, earlier called Országos Cigány Önkormányzat, has used the name Országos Roma Önkormányzat since around 2011.

Cigány has not disappeared. Many Roma call themselves cigány, some Roma organisations use it in their names, and it lives on in fixed terms such as cigányzene, cigányzenekar, oláhcigány and magyarcigány, which this lesson uses. Some people, Roma and non-Roma, hear the word as offensive, above all in a hostile context, while others see roma as a label from outside. Which word fits depends on who speaks, to whom and in what tone; in neutral writing about the community, roma is the safer choice.
